title: The born-free and the rest of us (1.19–1.22)
word: The born-free and the rest of us
hook: a few beings arrive at deep absorption by their very nature; for everyone else, Patanjali lists five things you need

segments.voice: Yesterday: samadhi with seed, absorption that still rests on something, and the kind that rests on nothing. With, without. What was your mind resting on? Today, who gets there, and how. Day four hundred thirty-five.

Every school has one. The kid who sits down at a piano at age four and just plays. The one who never studied and still aced the test. It's easy to look at them and decide that some people have it and others don't. Patanjali noticed that too, in his own way. In sutra 1.19 he admits that some beings reach a deep absorption by their very nature. And then, in 1.20, he turns to the rest of us, and doesn't sound worried at all.
screen: `THE KID WHO JUST PLAYS.` → `SOME HAVE IT, SOME DON'T?` → `PATANJALI TURNS TO THE REST OF US.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.19 names the born-free. For the bodiless ones and those merged in nature, the state arises from their very becoming, by birth, not effort. Who are they? The commentator Vyasa describes beings who have identified with the elements or with nature itself, and he adds a caution: their state looks like freedom, but it wears off, and they come back. So, in Vyasa's reading, the born-free aren't the goal. Sutra 1.20 is the main line. For everyone else, samadhi is preceded by five things: shraddha, faith, a settled trust that the path is real; virya, energy; smriti, memory, or mindfulness, keeping the aim in view; samadhi itself, the gathering; and prajna, wisdom. Notice that talent isn't on the list. Each of the five can be grown. Then 1.21: it is near for those whose urgency is intense. And 1.22 adds a wry detail. Even among the intense, there's a difference: mild, medium and intense. So: mild intensity, medium intensity, intense intensity. Commentators work out nine grades from these. It sounds like a scoreboard, but read it the other way round. One way to read it: in these sutras, how near the goal is depends on how much you care, not on what you were born with. Faith, energy, memory, gathering, wisdom. And then: how much do you want it?
screen: `THE BORN-FREE: BY NATURE.` · `THE REST: FIVE THINGS TO GROW.` · `NEAR FOR THE INTENSE.` · then, large: `MILD, MEDIUM, INTENSE.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Let's touch the five, one at a time, a few breaths each. Faith: notice whether there's any trust that sitting like this is worth it. Energy: lengthen the spine a little, wake up the body. Memory: remind yourself why you came to this practice at all. Gathering: rest on the breath. Wisdom: notice, without judging, how intense your wanting is today, mild, medium or intense. All of them are fine starting points. The bell holds the time.
The born-free and the rest of us. A few reach absorption by nature; everyone else by faith, energy, memory, gathering and wisdom, at whatever intensity they bring.
screen: `THE BORN-FREE AND THE REST OF US — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: mild, medium, intense. Pick one thing you care about. Rate your effort today honestly, mild, medium or intense, and turn it up one notch for an hour. Day four hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Yoga teachers often present shraddha, virya, smriti, samadhi and prajna as qualities to cultivate over a lifetime, and point to 1.21 to say that sincere intensity matters more than natural gifts.

pairs: memory: keeping the aim in view

myth: Vyasa treats the born-free as the goal of yoga
he says their state looks like freedom but wears off, and they return.
for everyone else, samadhi is preceded by faith, energy, memory, samadhi and wisdom
Patanjali says the goal is near for those with intense urgency

fork.setup: you weren't born a natural meditator. according to Patanjali, what decides how near the goal is?
options: the intensity of your wanting and effort.
fork.reveal: 1.21 says it is near for those whose urgency is intense, and 1.22 grades even that: mild, medium, intense.

original.note: Sanskrit śraddhā: faith, trust. the first of the five that come before samadhi in 1.20.

trapdoor: what you thought: some people are just born spiritual.
what it means: a few are, by nature, and it's a detour; everyone else grows five qualities, at the intensity they choose.
what a scholar hears: 1.19 is bhava-pratyaya (by birth) for videhas and prakriti-layas; 1.20 is upaya-pratyaya (by means); commentators combine 1.21–1.22 into nine grades of practitioner.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.19–1.22 (the born-free; faith, energy, memory, samadhi, wisdom; mild, medium, intense)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.19 (the videhas and prakriti-layas return)

notes: Editor review (y2 pass): the born-free no longer dismissed as 'a footnote' (Vyasa's reading named instead); the 'depends mostly on how much you care' line framed as one reading, not Patanjali's words; the practice no longer tells the listener what to feel.
Interpretation of videha and prakriti-laya varies widely among commentators; summarized from Vyasa. Some modern teachers read 'born-free' as those born with yogic attainment from past lives.
'Nine grades' from combining three levels of means with three of intensity: attributed to commentators generally; confirm (Vyasa and Vachaspati).
